                 DIRECT TESTIMONY OF AHMED FIGUEROA-SANTIAGO
                        ON BEHALF OF SAVE THE LAMPASAS

 1                                   I.       INTRODUCTION

 2     Q.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME.

 3     A.   My name is Ahmed Figueroa-Santiago.

 4     Q.   PLEASE STATE YOUR PROFESSIONAL BACKGROUND IN AVIATION

 5          SAFETY.

 6     A.   I am a retired Black Hawk helicopter pilot and Aviation Safety Manager for the Army.

 7          My rank was Chief Warrant Officer 3 (CW3) when I was medically separated/retired.

 8          I was formerly the Battalion Unit Trainer in charge of training all the training areas to

 9          include low level routes and corridors in and out of the restricted area from 2004-2008.

10          During that time I was also a Company Aviation Safety Officer. I also served as an

11          Operation Katrina Relieve Aviation Task Force Safety Officer and as a Battalion Safety

12          officer and Instructor Pilot for Camp Zama Japan in 2011. From 2008-2012, I was a

13          UH 60 Black Hawk Instructor Pilot at Fort Rucker Alabama. I am also a recipient of

14          Sikorsky rescue award for completing Sikorsky 1,000 combat hours. I have 1,500 flight

15          hours and 1,000 combat hours.


       CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                   AHMED FIGUEROA-SANTIAGO


                                                                                                         003
                                                                                           Page 4 of 9



 1   Q.   WAS YOUR FLIGHT TIME AS A PILOT FOR A PARTICULAR TYPE OF

 2        HELICOPTER?

 3   A.   Yes, specifically a Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk Helicopter used for Air Assault

 4        Airborne operations and rescue missions.

 5   Q.   WHAT HELICOPER DIVISIONS TRAIN AT FORT HOOD?

 6   A.   The primary active-duty aviation footprint at Fort Hood belongs to the 1st Cavalry

 7        Division, specifically operating under the 1st Air Cavalry Brigade (“Air Cav”).

 8        Because it is organized as a Heavy Combat Aviation Brigade (CAB), it fields a full

 9        spectrum of attack, reconnaissance, lift, and medical evacuation (MEDEVAC)

10        airframes. The primary helicopters stationed there and their specific subordinate units

11        include:

12               (1) AH-64E Apache (Attack/Reconnaissance). The Apache is the primary

13               attack and scout platform on the installation. It is fielded by two distinct

14               dynamic units within the brigade: 1st Battalion, 227th Aviation Regiment

15               (“First Attack”): An attack helicopter battalion utilizing the AH-64E variant for

16               precision strikes and close air support; and 7th Squadron, 17th Cavalry

17               Regiment (“PaleHorse”): An Air Cavalry Reconnaissance Squadron that

18               couples the Apache with unmanned aerial systems (UAS) for heavy scout and

19               tracking operations.

20               (2) UH-60M Black Hawk (Utility/Assault). The tactical workhorse for troop

21               transport, air assault, and command and control: 3rd Battalion, 227th Aviation

22               Regiment (“SpearHead”): An Assault Helicopter Battalion completely

23               dedicated to utility lift, air assault maneuvers, and rapid insertion.




     CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                   AHMED FIGUEROA-SANTIAGO


                                                                                                        004
                                                                                          Page 5 of 9



 1               (3) CH-47F Chinook & HH-60M Black Hawk (General Support &

 2               MEDEVAC). Heavy lift capabilities and dedicated medical evacuation fall

 3               under a multi-functional general support asset: 2nd Battalion, 227th Aviation

 4               Regiment (“Lobos”): A General Support Aviation Battalion (GSAB). It houses:

 5               CH-47F Chinooks for heavy-lift logistical transport, cargo, and mass troop

 6               movements; HH-60M Black Hawks, which are specially equipped medical

 7               variants dedicated entirely to aerial MEDEVAC operations; UH-60M

 8               configurations designated for Command and Control (C2) support.

 9   Q.   ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING?

10   A.   I am testifying on behalf of Save the Lampasas. I am a member of Save the Lampasas

11        and I live off CR 223 in the area that would be in the vicinity of Link G51.

12   Q.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

13   A.   To provide information addressing aircraft concerns in addition to those that were

14        raised in the direct testimony of other witnesses in this case.   Like the other members

15        of Save the Lampasas, Fort Hood and the safety of its personnel are important to our

16        community.

17   Q.   HAVE YOU EVER TESTIFIED AT THE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION

18        OF TEXAS BEFORE?

19   A.   No, I have not.

20   Q.   WAS THIS MATERIAL PREPARED BY YOU OR UNDER YOUR

21        SUPERVISION?

22   A.   Yes, it was.




     CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                    AHMED FIGUEROA-SANTIAGO


                                                                                                       005
                                                                                            Page 6 of 9


 1                                     II.      CONCERNS
 2   Q.   WITNESSES, INLCUDING D’ANDREA AND RHODES INDICATE THAT

 3        THE ROUTES THEY SUPPORT IS WARRANTED IN PART BECAUSE OF

 4        AERONAUTICAL SAFETY CONCERNS.                        ARE THERE AERONAUTICAL

 5        CONCERNS RELATED TO ROUTE 894 OR ANY ROUTE UTILIZING LINK

 6        G51?

 7   A.   Yes, Route 894 includes Link G51 which is the link that is the closest to the southwest

 8        portion of Fort Hood. Other witnesses supporting Route 894 offer testimony regarding

 9        impaired use of helicopters associated with other links. I have many concerns about

10        the potential impacts that any route using Link G52 would have on the tactical airspace

11        used for training at Fort Hood. First, the proposed routes create low-level flight and

12        maneuver obstacles and the material alteration of tactical airspace. The introduction of

13        765kV transmission infrastructure introduces permanent physical hazards into a

14        historically clear airspace, fundamentally degrading the established military training

15        routes. These lattice structures constitute significant vertical obstructions that

16        introduces an artificial “ceiling” to safe low-level operations, permanently modifying

17        the visual and physical profile of the local terrain.

18               Further, a 200-foot-wide cleared Right-of-Way (ROW) swath creates an

19        artificial linear landmark. This alters the natural terrain features that pilots rely on for

20        dead reckoning and visual terrain navigation, invalidating current tactical maps and

21        training baselines. In fact, Army helicopter doctrine requires proficiency in Terrain

22        Flight (TERF) profiles, specifically contour and Nap-of-the-Earth (NOE) flight

23        (navigating at or below treetop level utilizing natural valleys and depressions).

24        Inserting 200-foot physical clearing directly segments continuous tactical airspace, and




     CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                     AHMED FIGUEROA-SANTIAGO


                                                                                                         006
                                                                                             Page 7 of 9



 1        it forces aircraft out of covered, low-level profiles into higher, non-tactical altitudes,

 2        effectively neutralizing the realistic military value of the training corridor.

 3   Q.   WHAT CONCERNS DO YOU HAVE REGARDING THE TRANSMISSION

 4        LINE     ROUTE’S        POTETIAL         TO    GENERAL         ELECTROMAGNETIC

 5        INTERFERENCE (EMI)?

 6   A.   The intense electromagnetic radiation emitted by 765kV lines introduces invisible,

 7        compounding hazards that threaten the technological and sensory integrity of military

 8        aircraft. The high-voltage electromagnetic field creates a localized environment of

 9        high-strength EMI. This radiation has the potential to induce signal degradation, false

10        readings, or outright failure in critical, sensitive flight instruments. Affected systems

11        include radar altimeters (crucial for absolute altitude awareness during low-visibility

12        operations), Heads-Up Displays (HUDs), and ultra-high/very-high frequency

13        (UHF/VHF) communication arrays. In addition, high-voltage lines naturally generate

14        corona discharge—the ionization of surrounding air molecules. While invisible or faint

15        to the naked eye, this discharge emits energy that can cause “blooming” (severe visual

16        washing out) on Night Vision Goggles (NVGs). Because the central Texas training

17        fields are heavily utilized for nighttime tactical readiness, this visual distortion

18        significantly increases pilot cognitive load and directly degrades the safety margins

19        required for night vision operations.

20   Q.   WHAT SAFETY CONCERNS DO YOU HAVE REGARDING THE USE OF

21        LINK G51 ON HELICOPTERS?

22   A.   The physical composition of ultra-high-voltage transmission lines introduces high-

23        probability catalysts for spatial disorientation and dynamic flight mishaps.

24        Transmission shield wires (the highest wires spanning between towers to protect



     CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                    AHMED FIGUEROA-SANTIAGO


                                                                                                          007
                                                                                            Page 8 of 9



 1        against lightning) have an incredibly narrow cross-section and are notoriously difficult

 2        to visually detect from a moving cockpit. This invisibility is exacerbated during tactical

 3        maneuvers or environmental brownout/dust conditions typical of central Texas training

 4        grounds. When multi-aircraft formations encounter an unexpected or poorly visible

 5        200-foot structure, flight leads are forced to execute sudden, non-standard altitude

 6        adjustments. Forcing rapid vertical corrections within tight tactical formations

 7        introduces severe risks of spatial disorientation, loss of situational awareness, and mid-

 8        air collisions. Historically, military wire-strike incidents are high-fatality, catastrophic

 9        events resulting in the total loss of hull and crew. A summary document, included with

10        my testimony as Exhibit A, from a publicly available presentation of the Army provides

11        a good overview of consistent with these concerns regarding the importance of safety

12        and low-flying helicopter training in the area.

13   Q.   WHAT       OTHER       CONCERNS          DO    YOU      HAVE       REGARDING          THE

14        TRANSMISSION LINES IMPACT TO MILITARY TRAINING?

15   A.   The operational footprint of a 765kV line extends far beyond its physical 200-foot

16        ROW, imposing severe geographic restrictions on surrounding military land use. Due

17        to the combined threats of EMI and wire-strikes, the military must institute rigid, wide

18        no-fly buffer zones flanking the power line corridor. This effectively slices unified,

19        contiguous training areas into isolated, fragmented pockets. Large-scale air assault,

20        aerial refueling, or reconnaissance exercises requiring vast, unbroken expanses of

21        airspace become logistically impossible. Low-level tactical routes, emergency forced-

22        landing fields, and personnel/cargo Drop Zones (DZs) situated near the proposed path

23        would be rendered permanently non-viable. The proximity of these high-voltage lines

24        could violate standard military clearing distance criteria. This could force permanent



     CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                    AHMED FIGUEROA-SANTIAGO


                                                                                                         008
                                                                                         Page 9 of 9



 1        closure or costly relocation of critical training infrastructure, degrading the readiness

 2        of units stationed in the region.

 3   Q.   DID YOU USE ANY SOURCES IN REACHING THESE CONCLUSIONS?

 4   A.   Yes. My list of references is included as Exhibit B.

 5                                  III.      CONCLUSION

 6   Q.   PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR POSITION REGARDING THE ROUTING OF

 7        THE PROPOSED TRANSMISSION LINES.

 8   A.   Due to its proximity to Fort Hood, the proposed 765kV transmission line route using

 9        Link G51 cannot be viewed merely as a minor utility easement. It represents a

10        permanent, hazardous encroachment upon critical military training airspace. The

11        cumulative effects—ranging from fragmentation of training reserves, safety risks,

12        hazards caused by technological EMI disruptions, and material airspace training

13        degradation—will directly undermine tactical readiness and jeopardize the lives of

14        military aviators.

15   Q.   DOES THIS CONCLUDE YOUR DIRECT TESTIMONY?

16   A.   Yes, it does.




     CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                    AHMED FIGUEROA-SANTIAGO

                                                                                             Western Training Area
  • The Western Training Area (WTA) is a training space for American and NATO forces at Fort Cavazos in Texas. The WTA is
    more than 150 miles west of the installation and provides access to 15,900 square miles of airspace. The WTA is used for
    realistic training, including AH-64 Apache transition unit training and combined arms live fire exercises.




                                                                    WE ARE THE ARMY’S HOME

Trace Crawford, DAO, 254-287-8338, tracy.a.crawford8.civ@army.mil             4                                                014
                                                            Aircraft Ops in WTA Brief to TCUF
                                                                                                Background




    • Fort Cavazos aviation units operate AH-64, CH-47, and UH-60 “low and slow” rotary wing aircraft

    • Fort Cavazos Special Use Airspace alone is insufficient to meet Fort Cavazos aviation training and
      operational requirements

    • US Army aviation training manuals include requirements for terrain flight operations at or below 200” AGL

    • The WTA was originally established due to it including wide open expanses of sparsely populated land.
      Present day, the WTA has experienced population expansion and significant increases in livestock and
      exotic animal ranches

    • Fort Cavazos aviation units typically operate in the eastern portion of the WTA due to aircraft refuel
      considerations

    • Fort Cavazos has instituted “No Fly Areas” in the past, however, the administration of the process as well
      as the associated impact on the aviation training mission were significant

                                                                                                   Background




        14 Code of Federal Regulations: § 91.119 Minimum safe altitudes:


        Except when necessary for takeoff or landing, no person may operate an aircraft below the following
        altitudes:
        (a) Anywhere. An altitude allowing, if a power unit fails, an emergency landing without undue hazard to
        persons or property on the surface.
        (b) Over congested areas. Over any congested area of a city, town, or settlement, or over any open air
        assembly of persons, an altitude of 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000
        feet of the aircraft.
        (c) Over other than congested areas. An altitude of 500 feet above the surface, except over open water or
        sparsely populated areas. In those cases, the aircraft may not be operated closer than 500 feet to any
        person, vessel, vehicle, or structure.
        (d) Helicopters, powered parachutes, and weight-shift-control aircraft. If the operation is conducted without
        hazard to persons or property on the surface—
        (1) A helicopter may be operated at less than the minimums prescribed in paragraph (b) or (c) of this
        section, provided each person operating the helicopter complies with any routes or altitudes specifically
        prescribed for helicopters by the FAA

                                                                                                    Background




    Present Fort Cavazos Altitude Criteria:

                                                                    5-9. Altitudes

   a. Unless operations are in an approved under wire flight area, flights off the Fort Cavazos reservation will
   maintain a minimum altitude of at least 500 ft AGL with a 500 ft slant range from buildings, livestock, or other
   man-made obstructions.
   b. In WTAs 100, 110, and 111, tactical training below 500 ft AGL is discouraged due to the amount of civilian
   population. Battalion/Squadron/Squadron commanders or higher, may authorize tactical flight training below
   500 ft AGL.
   c. During WTA terrain flight operations at or below 200 ft AGL, aviators will not intentionally fly within a 500 ft
   slant range of buildings, livestock, or other manmade obstructions, except while performing an instrument
   approach or departure, during takeoff or landing, or when mission requirements dictate.
   d. Aided night operations below 200 ft AGL outside the FCRTAs require a day light reconnaissance of the
   intended flight route within 3 days of use.

                                                                                              Current Issue




       • Low Flying Aircraft / Noise Complaints within the WTA are on an upward trend commensurate with the
         level of aircraft operations in the WTA

       • There is a heightened level of volatility and organization amongst citizens in the WTA

       • Complainants within the WTA have filed high dollar claims for damage reimbursement and contacted
         local political leaders.

       • Many Low Flying Aircraft / Noise complainants believe they “own” the airspace above their property

                                                                                               Current Issue




    Questions Raised by Complainants:

    • What authority does Fort Cavazos have to fly helicopters over non-federal land?

    • Fort Cavazos is supposed to be one of the largest Army installations, so why can’t you do the training
      over your own land? How much land/space is required?

    • Why would your pilots deliberately target livestock? Why are they doing their maneuvers in an area when
      they can see livestock/homes/buildings, etc.? If they see livestock, can’t they just go to another area?

    • Why do they have to fly so low as to disrupt the livestock in the first place? Can’t they practice at a
      higher altitude?

    • These flights are happening at all times of the day and night – why?

    • They should have narrower flight corridors and conduct training out in West Texas or over the Gulf of
      Mexico where no one will be bothered. Why can’t they use areas that are less populated?

    • The government is impacting my livelihood. What are you going to do about that? I should be
      compensated for my loss.

                                                                    WE ARE THE ARMY’S HOME

Trace Crawford, DAO, 254-287-8338, tracy.a.crawford8.civ@army.mil            10                                  020
                                                            Aircraft Ops in WTA Brief to TCUF
                                                                                             Action Plan to Mitigate




    • Initiate community townhall / aircraft static displays in order to answer questions, discuss importance of
      aviation training, and ultimately foster relationships with WTA citizens. Gain Senior Commander guidance
      and intent prior to event

    • Conduct holistic review of Fort Cavazos 95-1 Local Flying Regulations to ensure WTA altitude and
      operational criteria encompasses “Fly Friendly” initiatives while ultimately enabling commanders to
      training and prepare their units for combat operations

    • Identify other training areas in the vicinity of Fort Cavazos to potentially “take the pressure off” WTA
      training areas 110 and 111.

    • Develop an installation Noise Hazard / Low Flying Aircraft complaint standard operating procedure
      specifying procedures, roles, and responsibilities

    • Determine the feasibility of “controlling” the level of aircraft operations in WTA 110 and 111 by means of a
      scheduling system

 5   Q.   WHAT HELICOPER DIVISIONS TRAIN AT FORT HOOD?

 6   A.   The primary active-duty aviation footprint at Fort Hood belongs to the 1 st Cavalry

 7        Division, specifically operating under the 1 st Air Cavalry Brigade ("Air Cav").

 8        Because it is organized as a Heavy Combat Aviation Brigade (CAB), it fields a full

 9        spectrum of attack, reconnaissance, lift, and medical evacuation (MEDEVAC)

10        airframes. The primary helicopters stationed there and their specific subordinate units

11        include:

12               (1)   AH-64E Apache (Attack/Reconnaissance). The Apache is the primary

13               attack and scout platform on the installation. It is fielded by two distinct

14               dynamic units within the brigade:       lst Battalion, 227th Aviation Regiment

15               ("First Attack"): An attack helicopter battalion utilizing the AH-64E variant for

16               precision strikes and close air support; and 7th Squadron, 17th Cavalry

17               Regiment ("PaleHorse"): An Air Cavalry Reconnaissance Squadron that

18               couples the Apache with unmanned aerial systems (UAS) for heavy scout and

19               tracking operations.

20               (2) UH-60M Black Hawk (Utility/Assault). The tactical workhorse for troop

21               transport, air assault, and command and control: 3rd Battalion, 227th Aviation

22               Regiment ("SpearHead"):        An Assault Helicopter Battalion completely

23               dedicated to utility lift, air assault maneuvers, and rapid insertion.

 1                                     n.       CONCERNS
 2   Q.   WITNESSES, INLCUDING D'ANDREA AND RHODES INDICATE THAT

 3        THE ROUTES THEY SUPPORT IS WARRANTED IN PART BECAUSE OF

 4        AERONAUTICAL SAFETY CONCERNS.                           ARE THERE AERONAUTICAL

 5        CONCERNS RELATED TO ROUTE 894 OR ANY ROUTE UTILIZING LINK

 6        G51?

 7   A.   Yes, Route 894 includes Link G5 1 which is the link that is the closest to the southwest

 8        portion ofFort Hood. Other witnesses supporting Route 894 offer testimony regarding

 9        impaired use of helicopters associated with other links. I have many concerns about

10        the potential impacts that any route using Link G52 would have on the tactical airspace

11        used for training at Fort Hood. First, the proposed routes create low-level flight and

12        maneuver obstacles and the material alteration of tactical airspace. The introduction of

13        765kV transmission infrastructure introduces permanent physical hazards into a

14        historically clear airspace, fundamentally degrading the established military training

15        routes. These lattice structures constitute significant vertical obstructions that

16        introduces an artificial "ceiling" to safe low-level operations, permanently modifying

17        the visual and physical profile of the local terrain.

18                Further, a 200-foot-wide cleared Right-of-Way (ROW) swath creates an

19        artificial linear landmark. This alters the natural terrain features that pilots rely on for

20        dead reckoning and visual terrain navigation, invalidating current tactical maps and

21        training baselines. In fact, Army helicopter doctrine requires proficiency in Terrain

22        Flight (TERF) profiles, specifically contour and Nap-of-the-Earth (NOE) flight

23        (navigating at or below treetop level utilizing natural valleys and depressions).

24        Inserting 200-foot physical clearing directly segments continuous tactical airspace, and

 3   Q.   WHAT CONCERNS DO YOU HAVE REGARDING THE TRANSMISSION

 4        LINE     ROUTE'S        POTETIAL         TO     GENERAL         ELECTROMAGNETIC

 5        INTERFERENCE (EMI)?

 6   A.   The intense electromagnetic radiation emitted by 765kV lines introduces invisible,

 7        compounding hazards that threaten the technological and sensory integrity of military

 8        aircraft. The high-voltage electromagnetic field creates a localized environment of

 9        high-strength EMI. This radiation has the potential to induce signal degradation, false

10        readings, or outright failure in critical, sensitive flight instruments. Affected systems

11        include radar altimeters (crucial for absolute altitude awareness during low-visibility

12        operations),   Heads-Up Displays        (HUI)s),   and ultra-high/very-high frequency

13        (UHF/VHF) communication arrays. In addition, high-voltage lines naturally generate

14        corona discharge-the ionization of surrounding air molecules. While invisible or faint

15        to the naked eye, this discharge emits energy that can cause "blooming" (severe visual

16        washing out) on Night Vision Goggles (NVGs). Because the central Texas training

17        fields are heavily utilized for nighttime tactical readiness, this visual distortion

18        significantly increases pilot cognitive load and directly degrades the safety margins

19        required for night vision operations.

20   Q.   WHAT SAFETY CONCERNS DO YOU HAVE REGARDING THE USE OF

21        LINK G51 ON HELICOPTERS?

22   A.   The physical composition of ultra-high-voltage transmission lines introduces high-

23        probability catalysts for spatial disorientation and dynamic flight mishaps.

24        Transmission shield wires (the highest wires spanning between towers to protect




     CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                     AHMED FIGUEROA-SANTIAGO
                                                                                            Page 8 of 9



 1        against lightning) have an incredibly narrow cross-section and are notoriously difficult

 2        to visually detect from a moving cockpit. This invisibility is exacerbated during tactical

 3        maneuvers or environmental brownout/dust conditions typical of central Texas training

 4        grounds. When multi-aircraft formations encounter an unexpected or poorly visible

 5        200-foot structure, flight leads are forced to execute sudden, non-standard altitude

 6        adjustments. Forcing rapid vertical corrections within tight tactical formations

 7        introduces severe risks of spatial disorientation, loss of situational awareness, and mid-

 8        air collisions. Historically, military wire-strike incidents are high-fatality, catastrophic

 9        events resulting in the total loss of hull and crew. A summary document, included with

10        my testimony as Exhibit A, from a publicly available presentation ofthe Army provides

11        a good overview of consistent with these concerns regarding the importance of safety

12        and low-flying helicopter training in the area.

13   Q.   WHAT       OTHER       CONCERNS          DO    YOU      HAVE       REGARDING          THE

14        TRANSMISSION LINES IMPACT TO MILITARY TRAINING?

15   A.   The operational footprint of a 765kV line extends far beyond its physical 200-foot

16        ROW, imposing severe geographic restrictions on surrounding military land use. Due

17        to the combined threats of EMI and wire-strikes, the military must institute rigid, wide

18        no-fly buffer zones flanking the power line corridor. This effectively slices unified,

19        contiguous training areas into isolated, fragmented pockets. Large-scale air assault,

20        aerial refueling, or reconnaissance exercises requiring vast, unbroken expanses of

21        airspace become logistically impossible. Low-level tactical routes, emergency forced-

22        landing fields, and personnel/cargo Drop Zones (DZs) situated near the proposed path

23        would be rendered permanently non-viable. The proximity of these high-voltage lines

24        could violate standard military clearing distance criteria. This could force permanent

 5                                   III.     CONCLUSION

 6   Q.   PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR POSITION REGARDING THE ROUTING OF

 7        THE PROPOSED TRANSMISSION LINES.

 8   A.   Due to its proximity to Fort Hood, the proposed 765kV transmission line route using

 9        Link G51 cannot be viewed merely as a minor utility easement. It represents a

10        permanent, hazardous encroachment upon critical military training airspace. The

11        cumulative effects-ranging from fragmentation of training reserves, safety risks,

12        hazards caused by technological EMI disruptions, and material airspace training

13        degradation-will directly undermine tactical readiness and j eopardize the lives of

14        military aviators.

16   A.   Yes, it does.

                                                                                                    Background




         Fort Cavazos aviation units operate AH-64, CH-47, and UH-60 "low and slow" rotary wing aircraft

         Fort Cavazos Special Use Airspace alone is insufficient to meet Fort Cavazos aviation training and
         operational requirements
         US Army aviation training manuals include requirements for terrain flight operations at or below 200" AGL

         The WTA was originally established due to it including wide open expanses of sparsely populated land.
         Present day, the WTA has experienced population expansion and significant increases in livestock and
         exotic animal ranches
         Fort Cavazos aviation units typically operate in the eastern portion of the WTA due to aircraft refuel
         considerations
         Fort Cavazos has instituted "No Fly Areas" in the past, however, the administration of the process as well
         as the associated impact on the aviation training mission were significant

        14 Code of Federal Regulations: § 91.119 Minimum safe altitudes:


        Except when necessary for takeoff or landing, no person may operate an aircraft below the following
        altitudes:
        (a) Anywhere. An altitude allowing, if a power unit fails, an emergency landing without undue hazard to
        persons or property on the surface.
        (b) Over congested areas. Over any congested area of a city, town, or settlement, or over any open air
        assembly of persons, an altitude of 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000
        feet of the aircraft.
        (c) Over other than congested areas. An altitude of 500 feet above the surface, except over open water or
        sparsely populated areas. In those cases, the aircraft may not be operated closer than 500 feet to any
        person, vessel, vehicle, or structure.
        (d) Helicopters, powered parachutes, and weight-shift-control aircraft. If the operation is conducted without~
        hazard to persons or property on the surface-
        (1) A helicopter may be operated at less than the minimums prescribed in paragraph (b) or (c) of this
        section, provided each person operating the helicopter complies with any routes or altitudes specifically
        prescribed for helicopters by the FAA

                                                                                                    Background




    Present Fort Cavazos Altitude Criteria:

                                                                    5-9. Altitudes

   a. Unless operations are in an approved under wire flight area, flights off the Fort Cavazos reservation will
   maintain a minimum altitude of at least 500 ft AGL with a 500 ft slant range from buildings, livestock, or other
   man-made obstructions.
   b. In WTAs 100, 110, and 111, tactical training below 500 ft AGL is discouraged due to the amount of civilian
   population. Battalion/Squadron/Squadron commanders or higher, may authorize tactical flight training below
   500 ft AGL.
   c. During WTA terrain flight operations at or below 200 ft AGL, aviators will not intentionally fly within a 500 ft
   slant range of buildings, livestock, or other manmade obstructions, except while performing an instrument
   approach or departure, during takeoff or landing, or when mission requirements dictate.
   d. Aided night operations below 200 ft AGL outside the FCRTAs require a day light reconnaissance of the
   intended flight route within 3 days of use.

    Questions Raised by Complainants:

         What authority does Fort Cavazos have to fly helicopters over non-federal land?

         Fort Cavazos is supposed to be one of the Iargest Army installations, so why can't you do the training
         over your own land? How much land/space is required?

         Why would your pilots deliberately target livestock? Why are they doing their maneuvers in an area when
         they can see livestock/homes/buildings, etc.? If they see livestock, can't they just go to another area?

         Why do they have to fly so low as to disrupt the livestock in the first place? Can't they practice at a
         higher altitude?
         These flights are happening at all times of the day and night - why?

         They should have narrower flight corridors and conduct training out in West Texas or over the Gulf of
         Mexico where no one will be bothered. Why can't they use areas that are less populated?

         The government is impacting my Iivelihood. What are you going to do about that? I should be
         compensated for my loss.
